paragraphs: Canonical correlation analysis, or CCA, finds lower-dimensional representations of two sets of variables that are maximally correlated. For classification, one set can describe the examples while the other comes from their labels. This makes CCA a way to reduce the number of input dimensions while retaining relationships with the prediction task.

The paper connects CCA to least squares, an optimization problem based on minimizing squared discrepancies. This connection was already known for binary classification. The authors extend it to multi-label classification under a mild condition that tends to hold for high-dimensional data. The condition matters: the claimed equivalence is not presented as applying to every possible dataset.

That equivalence provides a route to modifying CCA through familiar least-squares techniques. The proposed extensions include sparse CCA with 1-norm regularization. Experiments on multi-label datasets support the equivalence and demonstrate the effectiveness of the extensions, showing that the reformulation offers both a conceptual connection and a practical basis for new methods.
icml-2008-a-least-squares-formulation-fo.tldr: Under a mild condition, multi-label CCA becomes a least-squares problem, enabling extensions such as sparse CCA.

paragraphs: Policy evaluation estimates the value of following a particular policy. Least-squares temporal difference methods had shown good practical performance on this task, but the statistical quality of their estimates was less well understood. This paper studies that quality through semiparametric statistical inference, connecting a reinforcement learning procedure to a framework for analyzing estimators.

The authors show that an LSTD-based estimator can be obtained from a particular estimating function. This construction guarantees convergence to the true value asymptotically, without requiring a specified model of the environment. The result concerns what happens as the available information grows, rather than asserting that every estimate from a limited sample is exact.

The paper then analyzes asymptotic variance, which describes the estimator's remaining variability in that large-sample setting. It derives an optimal estimating function with minimum asymptotic estimation variance. Because obtaining that function carries a computational burden, the authors also derive a suboptimal estimator intended to reduce the cost. The contribution therefore links estimation quality with the computation needed to pursue it.
icml-2008-a-semiparametric-statistical-a.tldr: A statistical analysis of LSTD policy evaluation yields a minimum-asymptotic-variance estimating function and a less costly suboptimal estimator.

paragraphs: Multiple instance learning assigns labels to bags containing several instances. A central question is how the instances together determine a bag's label. The paper argues that this relationship varies across application domains and need not follow traditional multiple instance learning assumptions. A rule suitable for one domain can therefore be an inappropriate starting point for another.

The authors propose learning the domain-specific relationship from labeled bags alone. Their framework uses mixture models to describe each bag's composition and an adaptable kernel to express relationships between bags. This makes the connection between bag contents and labels something the method can adapt, rather than a mechanism that must be fixed in advance.

Experiments on synthetic datasets validate the kernel's ability to adapt to different mechanisms for producing bag labels. The paper also compares the approach with established methods on real-world benchmarks, although the abstract states no comparative outcome for those tests. The motivating use case is a new application where the mechanism connecting instances to bag labels is unknown.
icml-2008-adaptive-p-posterior-mixture-m.tldr: Mixture models and an adaptable kernel let multiple instance learning infer domain-specific relationships between bag contents and labels.

paragraphs: Multi-view semi-supervised learning uses several representations of the same examples. The methods considered here learn a prediction function for each view, encourage agreement on unlabeled examples, and require their average prediction to fit labeled examples. Agreement gives the unlabeled data a role in shaping the learned functions.

The paper combines this arrangement into a single reproducing kernel Hilbert space, or RKHS, with a data-dependent norm encoding co-regularization. Its kernel can be derived explicitly and used in any kernel method. Once this construction is made, the learning problem takes the form of standard supervised learning, while the kernel retains the influence of the unlabeled examples and multiple views.

This reformulation also makes existing tools for bounding model complexity directly applicable, including more refined localized bounds. The authors propose an alternative to manifold regularization and report major empirical improvements on semi-supervised tasks. Their formulation naturally predicts on unseen test examples, extending its use beyond assigning labels only to the points already included during training.
icml-2008-an-rkhs-for-multi-view-learnin.tldr: A single data-dependent kernel captures multi-view co-regularization, enabling standard kernel methods, existing theory, and prediction on unseen examples.

paragraphs: Apprenticeship learning tries to learn a policy that performs at least as well as an expert's demonstrated policy. The setting is a Markov decision process whose true reward function is assumed unknown. That missing reward makes the task different from simply optimizing a known measure of success: expert behavior supplies the reference for learning.

The paper formulates apprenticeship learning as a linear program. This allows the problem to be solved with an off-the-shelf optimization solver. In the reported experiments, the approach substantially reduces running time relative to existing methods, with improvements reaching two orders of magnitude. That figure describes the experimental speedup, rather than a guaranteed speedup for every problem.

The formulation also produces stationary policies. The methods discussed as existing alternatives instead output mixed policies, meaning randomized combinations of stationary policies. The authors additionally present a technique general enough to convert any mixed policy into a stationary one. The work therefore changes both the computational route to apprenticeship learning and the form of the resulting policy.
icml-2008-apprenticeship-learning-using-.tldr: A linear-programming formulation produces stationary apprenticeship policies and runs up to two orders of magnitude faster in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: A support vector machine ordinarily starts with a chosen kernel, which determines how examples are compared during learning. Multiple kernel learning adds flexibility by optimizing a combination of basis kernels. This paper addresses a further structure in that choice: kernels may belong to groups because they arise from distinct components of the data.

Composite Kernel Learning incorporates those groups into the learning formulation. The framework covers several setups that place different amounts of emphasis on group structure. This matters when the relationships among candidate kernels are meaningful, because the learning problem can reflect those relationships as well as the individual kernels available for combination.

The authors characterize the convexity of the resulting optimization problem and provide a general wrapper algorithm for computing solutions. They illustrate the method with multi-channel data, where each channel corresponds to a group of kernels. The stated contribution is a flexible formulation and a way to solve it, together with an illustration of its behavior; the abstract does not claim a universal accuracy advantage.
icml-2008-composite-kernel-learning-76ef.tldr: Composite Kernel Learning extends multiple kernel learning to account for meaningful groups among candidate kernels.

paragraphs: The paper connects nonlinear embedding methods used in shallow semi-supervised learning with deep, multi-layer architectures. Its starting point is that embedding algorithms already used with approaches such as kernel methods can also help shape a deep model. The contribution is a way to apply those existing ideas within a different kind of architecture.

The embedding can act as a regularizer at the output layer, or regularization can be applied at every layer. These choices determine where the embedding influences learning: at the final output or throughout the sequence of intermediate representations. The paper therefore offers more than one place to incorporate semi-supervised embedding into a deep architecture.

The authors describe this as a simple alternative to existing deep learning approaches and report competitive error rates. The comparisons cover both other deep methods and shallow semi-supervised techniques. Competitive performance supports the usefulness of this connection between embedding and deep learning, while stopping short of claiming that the approach consistently outperforms either class of alternatives.
icml-2008-deep-learning-via-semi-supervi.tldr: Nonlinear semi-supervised embeddings can regularize deep networks at the output or throughout their layers, yielding competitive error rates.

paragraphs: A complicated function becomes easier to understand when it can be written as a sum of simpler components, each involving fewer variables. Interactions complicate that picture: some variables have joint effects that cannot be represented additively and must be modeled together. The paper focuses on detecting these statistical interactions.

Its strategy compares two prediction models. One can represent the interaction being investigated; the other is explicitly prevented from representing it. Comparing their predictive performance provides a way to assess the importance of allowing that joint effect. The key design requirement is a model family whose restrictions can target the interaction in question.

The authors show that Additive Groves, a regression ensemble based on an additive model, can be restricted in the required way. This gives the ensemble the properties needed for accurate interaction detection within their framework. The contribution connects prediction and interpretation: model comparisons are used to investigate which variables need to be understood jointly when describing a complex function.
icml-2008-detecting-statistical-interact.tldr: Comparing unrestricted Additive Groves with versions that forbid a particular interaction provides a framework for detecting joint variable effects.

paragraphs: Compositional data consists of positive components whose sum is fixed. When there are many components and complicated relationships among them, dimensionality reduction is attractive. The difficulty is that the smaller representation must respect the data's constraints and statistical properties. The paper identifies these requirements as a reason traditional techniques such as PCA are unsuitable for the problems considered.

The proposed method first identifies a family of projections that preserve the relevant compositional constraints. It then chooses the projection that maximizes estimated Dirichlet precision in the projected data. Thus, the optimization takes place within a family of representations already designed to remain valid for compositional data.

The result has a specified lower dimensionality, with its components decorrelated as much as possible under the approach. The authors develop a theoretical foundation and validate effectiveness on synthetic and real-world datasets. The central contribution is to treat constraint preservation and reduction of component dependence as connected parts of feature extraction, rather than handling dimensionality alone.
icml-2008-dirichlet-component-analysis-f.tldr: Dirichlet component analysis reduces compositional data while preserving its constraints and seeking components that are as decorrelated as possible.

paragraphs: A Bayesian network classifier needs parameters as well as a network structure. This paper considers parameter learning when the structure is already fixed. It describes a practical tradeoff between generative learning, which is more efficient, and discriminative learning, which is more effective for classification. The goal is to combine these desirable properties.

The proposed method, Discriminative Frequency Estimate, learns parameters by computing frequencies from the data in a discriminative way. Frequency estimation is therefore the central mechanism through which the authors pursue classification effectiveness without the computational expense associated with the discriminative alternative considered. The contribution concerns how parameters are learned within the given network.

Empirical studies compare DFE with ELR, identified as a state-of-the-art discriminative parameter learning method. DFE achieves comparable classification accuracy while being significantly more efficient in those studies. This supports the authors' claim that the method combines advantages of the two learning approaches: the result is an observed accuracy-efficiency tradeoff, rather than a claim that DFE is always more accurate.
icml-2008-discriminative-parameter-learn.tldr: Discriminative Frequency Estimate matches ELR's accuracy in empirical studies while learning Bayesian network parameters significantly more efficiently.

paragraphs: Learning a deep model can be helped by an initial unsupervised stage that turns inputs into useful intermediate representations. This paper introduces a training principle for that stage: learned representations should remain useful when part of the input has been corrupted. Robustness to partial corruption becomes a goal of representation learning itself.

The principle can be used to train denoising autoencoders. These models can then be stacked to initialize a deeper architecture, allowing representations learned at successive stages to be composed. The paper motivates this approach from several perspectives, including manifold learning, information theory, and generative modeling, connecting the same training idea to different ways of understanding representation learning.

Comparative experiments on a suite of pattern classification benchmarks show an advantage from corrupting autoencoder inputs during training. The finding gives practical support to the proposed principle: deliberately damaging part of the input can help produce features that serve a later classification task. The reported advantage concerns the benchmark comparisons, rather than a guarantee for every kind of corruption or dataset.
icml-2008-extracting-and-composing-robus.tldr: Training autoencoders to handle partially corrupted inputs produces useful representations that can be stacked to initialize deep models.

paragraphs: Nearest neighbor classification depends on how distance is measured. This paper works within large margin nearest neighbor learning, or LMNN, which learns a Mahalanobis distance metric to improve classification. Its focus is making that framework scale to large datasets and adapt to differences across the input space.

The first contribution is an efficient solver for the particular semidefinite optimization problem arising in LMNN. The authors report handling problems with billions of large margin constraints in a few hours. They also use metric ball trees to reduce training and testing times, with further speedups when the learned representation has fewer dimensions.

A third contribution allows different parts of the input space to use different learned distance metrics. These mixtures of locally adaptive metrics achieve lower error rates on large datasets in the reported work. Together, the contributions address two distinct needs: reducing the computational expense of learning and using distances, and making those distances more responsive to local structure.
icml-2008-fast-solvers-and-efficient-imp.tldr: Efficient optimization, metric ball trees, and locally adaptive distances make LMNN more scalable and improve its reported classification performance.

paragraphs: Graph transduction labels data using a graph connecting labeled and unlabeled examples, encouraging predictions to vary smoothly along that graph. Existing methods can be sensitive to the initial labels, particularly when labels are weak, classes are imbalanced, or labeled examples are not selected randomly. Early labeling mistakes can affect later propagation.

The paper introduces an objective that jointly involves a prediction function on the graph and a binary label matrix. It generalizes earlier objectives and adds node normalization terms intended to improve resilience to class imbalance. Because globally minimizing the objective is intractable, the authors use alternating minimization to adjust the function and labels incrementally toward a reliable local minimum.

This procedure avoids prematurely committing to erroneous labels and produces more consistent labeling in the reported work. Experiments include synthetic tasks and real digit and text recognition problems. The authors report substantial accuracy improvements over state-of-the-art semi-supervised methods, with especially pronounced advantages when few labeled examples are available. These are empirical gains from an approach explicitly targeting local optimization.
icml-2008-graph-transduction-via-alterna.tldr: Alternately updating graph predictions and labels improves reported transduction accuracy, especially with few labeled examples.

paragraphs: Manifold alignment seeks to connect representations from different domains so that knowledge can transfer between them. This paper introduces an approach based on Procrustes analysis. Its emphasis is both on aligning the available data and on obtaining a mapping that can be used beyond the particular examples supplied during training.

The scope of that mapping is a central distinction. When paired with a suitable dimensionality reduction method, the approach produces a mapping defined everywhere, rather than only at the training points. The qualification is essential: this extension depends on the dimensionality reduction method used. It makes the choice of representation part of what enables the alignment to generalize.

The authors study the approach theoretically and experimentally, reporting useful knowledge transfer between domains. Applications include cross-lingual information retrieval and transfer learning in Markov decision processes. These examples show the alignment idea being used in different kinds of transfer tasks, while the broader contribution is a route to mappings that remain usable outside the original training set.
icml-2008-manifold-alignment-using-procr.tldr: Procrustes-based manifold alignment enables useful knowledge transfer and, with suitable dimensionality reduction, mappings beyond training points.

paragraphs: A smoothing kernel classifier depends on both the distance between examples and the kernel's bandwidth. This paper proposes learning those choices together to improve classification. The learned distance comes from a function that maps an arbitrary metric space into a Euclidean space, making the geometry used by the classifier depend on the data.

The embedding is learned by minimizing an upper bound on the classifier's resubstitution error estimate, which evaluates error using the training examples. Restricting the embedding function to a reproducing kernel Hilbert space turns the problem into a semidefinite program. The authors also show that the resulting classification rule is a variation of the k-nearest neighbor rule.

On benchmark datasets, the proposed rule achieves accuracy that is better than or comparable to the tested state-of-the-art metric learning algorithms designed for nearest neighbor classification. These results support jointly learning the distance and smoothing behavior in the evaluated settings. The optimization objective itself concerns an upper bound on a training-based error estimate, distinct from the reported benchmark comparisons.
icml-2008-metric-embedding-for-kernel-cl.tldr: Learning a Euclidean embedding and kernel bandwidth together yields a classifier with competitive or better accuracy in the reported metric-learning comparisons.

paragraphs: The nu-support vector classifier has a parameter with an intuitive interpretation: nu roughly describes the fraction of support vectors. Yet the original formulation does not allow every value between zero and one. That mismatch between interpretation and permitted values motivates the extension considered in this paper.

An earlier non-convex extension resolved the parameter-range issue and had shown better generalization experimentally than the original classifier. However, the reasons for its generalization behavior and the convergence properties of its optimization algorithm had not been established. The paper addresses those theoretical questions, connecting observed performance with the need to understand how the algorithm behaves.

The authors provide new theoretical insights and propose a new nu-SVC algorithm with guarantees for both generalization performance and convergence. The title frames the work through conditional value-at-risk minimization. The stated advance is therefore a theoretically supported algorithm for this classification setting; the abstract does not claim that the new method universally improves accuracy or specify the precise form of its guarantees.
icml-2008-nu-support-vector-machine-as-c.tldr: The paper develops theoretical support for extended nu-SVC and proposes an algorithm with generalization and convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: The paper studies how many labeled examples multi-view active learning needs to reach a target error rate. Its main theoretical result holds under an alpha-expansion assumption. With that assumption, the sample complexity improves from roughly inverse dependence on the target error to logarithmic dependence, with additional logarithmic factors suppressed in the stated notation.

The authors describe this as an exponential improvement. Their result does not require the particular strong restrictions mentioned in the abstract, such as uniformly distributed data on a unit sphere or classifiers restricted to linear separators through the origin. It still depends on alpha-expansion. When that assumption fails, the paper separately supplies an upper bound on the error rate.

The authors then analyze combining multi-view active learning with semi-supervised learning and obtain a further sample-complexity improvement. They also study the combination empirically and report evidence of its efficiency. The contribution thus connects a conditional theoretical reduction in label requirements with experimental support for using the two learning paradigms together.
icml-2008-on-multi-view-active-learning-.tldr: Under alpha-expansion, multi-view active learning sharply reduces label requirements, with further gains from combining it with semi-supervised learning.

paragraphs: The paper studies prediction with expert advice in the setting called the Brier game. The central question is how to construct a prediction algorithm with a theoretical performance guarantee. Rather than presenting only an application, the authors establish a mathematical property of the prediction game and use it to derive an algorithm.

They prove that the Brier game is mixable and identify its optimal learning rate and substitution function. These are the ingredients used to form the resulting prediction procedure. The optimality claim applies to those ingredients in this setting, giving the algorithm a principled specification rather than merely reporting a successful choice from an application.

The algorithm is applied to football and tennis match prediction. On these datasets, the theoretical guarantee is reported to be fairly tight, especially on the larger tennis dataset. This means the guarantee closely reflects the observed performance in those applications. The empirical contribution is therefore evidence about the practical informativeness of the theory, not just an example of deploying the algorithm.
icml-2008-prediction-with-expert-advice-.tldr: The Brier game's mixability yields a prediction algorithm whose theoretical guarantee is fairly tight on football and especially tennis data.

paragraphs: Search and learning can both estimate how valuable a game state is, but they retain that information differently. Search may build an estimate for the current move and then discard it. Learning can accumulate estimates across many moves and games. Dyna-2 brings these activities into one reinforcement learning architecture while keeping their memories separate.

Both the transient planning memory and the permanent learning memory use linear function approximation and are updated with Sarsa. This lets both learning and search generalize across states. For 9-by-9 Go, the authors use a million binary features based on templates matching small board fragments, giving both memories a shared kind of representation.

Using only transient memory, Dyna-2 performs at least as well as UCT in the reported comparison. Combining both memories significantly outperforms UCT. The resulting program also achieves a higher Computer Go Online Server rating than any handcrafted or traditional search-based program. These findings support the practical value of combining accumulated learning with temporary planning in this Go setting.
icml-2008-sample-based-learning-and-sear.tldr: Dyna-2 combines separate temporary planning and persistent learning memories, significantly outperforming UCT in the reported 9-by-9 Go comparison.

paragraphs: Sparse Gaussian process methods reduce computation by using a limited number of basis functions. Common constructions obtain those functions by fixing one input of the covariance function. This paper makes the basis functions more flexible for Gaussian covariance functions, allowing each Gaussian basis function to have an arbitrary diagonal covariance matrix, or its own length scales.

For a fixed number of basis functions, the richer family permits approximations that are no worse, and typically better, under a given criterion. This is a statement about the flexibility of the approximation family. The authors fit the model through gradient-based marginal likelihood optimization, with a stated time cost of O(m²n), where m counts basis functions and n counts data points.

Comparisons with other sparse Gaussian process methods favor the proposed approach, particularly when very few basis functions are used. The paper also presents results for support vector machines and kernel ridge regression. Although Gaussian process regression is the main focus, the authors identify the flexible-basis idea as applicable more broadly to kernel-based algorithms.
icml-2008-sparse-multiscale-gaussian-pro.tldr: Giving sparse Gaussian basis functions independent length scales improves approximation flexibility and reported performance, especially with very few basis functions.

paragraphs: Moment matching estimates a probability distribution by making selected summaries of the estimate agree with those of the target distribution. The paper extends this familiar approach from parametric density estimation to nonparametric estimation of mixture models. Its focus is on choosing a representation in which the matching operation becomes useful for a particular class of functions.

The method embeds distributions into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space and matches moments there. This allows the density estimator to be tailored to functions whose expectations the user wants to compute. The target function class therefore helps determine what the estimated distribution should preserve, linking density estimation to the calculations that will later use it.

The authors demonstrate usefulness in message compression for graphical models and in image classification and retrieval. These applications illustrate how the same distribution-matching approach can support different tasks. The stated contribution is a way to adapt density estimation to a function class of interest, together with evidence of usefulness in the named applications.
icml-2008-tailoring-density-estimation-v.tldr: Matching distribution embeddings in a kernel space tailors nonparametric mixture density estimates to the functions whose expectations matter.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning aims to make supervised learning more efficient by also using examples without labels. The paper focuses on discriminative probabilistic models, for which incorporating unlabeled data is described as challenging. Its question is how to make those additional examples contribute through the objective used to learn the model.

The authors introduce a methodology built around a simple semi-supervised objective function. This objective defines an estimator that uses unlabeled information, giving a concrete mathematical route for bringing semi-supervised learning into the discriminative setting. The contribution is thus both a proposed learning objective and an analysis of the estimator associated with it.

The main stated result proves that the estimator is asymptotically optimal. That is a large-sample claim, so it should not be read as a promise of optimal behavior for every finite dataset. The paper discusses the practical consequences specifically for logistic regression, connecting the theoretical result to a concrete model. Its significance is the combination of an accessible objective construction with a formal asymptotic justification.
icml-2008-the-asymptotics-of-semi-superv.tldr: A simple semi-supervised objective yields an asymptotically optimal estimator for discriminative probabilistic modeling, with implications discussed for logistic regression.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning must balance exploring uncertain possibilities with exploiting behavior that already appears useful. The paper focuses on two ideas used in advanced exploration methods: optimism under uncertainty and building a model. Its aim is to integrate several concepts into an algorithm that is both fast and simple.

The theoretical result states that the proposed algorithm finds a near-optimal policy in polynomial time. This connects the exploration strategy to a formal claim about both policy quality and computational growth. Near-optimality allows some gap from the best policy, while polynomial time characterizes the guarantee's computational scale rather than specifying a fixed running time.

The authors also provide experimental evidence that the algorithm is robust and efficient compared with its predecessors. These experiments complement the theory by examining practical behavior relative to the methods from which the approach develops. The contribution is a unified exploration algorithm with a polynomial-time near-optimality result and supporting empirical evidence, rather than a claim to resolve every exploration problem.
icml-2008-the-many-faces-of-optimism-a-u.tldr: A unified optimism-based exploration algorithm finds a near-optimal policy in polynomial time and shows empirical robustness and efficiency.

paragraphs: Dimensionality reduction commonly places data in a Euclidean latent space. The paper argues that this geometry is inappropriate for some datasets. Human motion provides the motivating example: its latent structure may be better represented by a cylinder or torus, shapes that an ordinary Euclidean latent space captures poorly.

The authors present several approaches for embedding data into non-Euclidean latent spaces, focusing on the Gaussian Process latent variable model. The choice of latent-space structure is part of the model design. It determines the kind of representation available for organizing motion data and for interpreting directions of variation within that representation.

In human motion modeling, the resulting models have interpretable latent directions that can support separating style from content. They also generalize beyond the dataset by learning transitions between motion styles even when those transitions are absent from the data. The stated significance is both interpretability and this particular form of generalization, enabled by using latent spaces better suited to the motion structure.
icml-2008-topologically-constrained-late.tldr: Non-Euclidean latent spaces support interpretable human-motion models and transitions between styles absent from the training data.

paragraphs: The paper introduces Persistent Contrastive Divergence, a training algorithm for Restricted Boltzmann Machines. Its key distinction from standard Contrastive Divergence is the sampling objective: it aims to obtain samples from almost exactly the model's distribution. This places the quality of the samples used during learning at the center of the proposed change.

The authors compare the algorithm with standard Contrastive Divergence methods on two digit-related tasks. One is modeling handwritten digits. The other is classifying digit images by learning a joint distribution over images and labels. These tasks examine the training method in both a data-modeling role and a classification setting built around a learned joint model.

Persistent Contrastive Divergence outperforms the comparison algorithms in the reported study while remaining equally fast and simple. The finding matters because the observed improvement does not come with a reported increase in those practical costs. The sampling description remains an aim of the algorithm, while the stronger performance claim is grounded in the digit experiments presented.
icml-2008-training-restricted-boltzmann-.tldr: Persistent Contrastive Divergence improves reported RBM digit-modeling and classification results while remaining as fast and simple as the compared methods.
